# Effects of substrate temperature on graphene nucleation density

## Abstract

We report chemical vapor deposition growth of graphene on copper foil across a substrate
temperature range of 950 to 1050 degrees Celsius. Nucleation density decreased by two orders of
magnitude over this range, consistent with a thermally activated attachment barrier. Domain size
correlated inversely with nucleation density, and single-crystal domains exceeding 200 micrometers
were obtained at the highest temperatures tested.

## Methods

Copper foil substrates were annealed under hydrogen flow for 30 minutes prior to growth. Methane was
introduced at a partial pressure of 50 millitorr, and growth proceeded for 20 minutes at each set
point. Five substrates were processed per temperature, and domain counts were obtained by scanning
electron microscopy over a fixed 1 square millimeter field.

## Results

Table 1 summarizes nucleation density as a function of temperature. The relationship is well
described by an Arrhenius model, with an apparent activation energy of 2.3 electronvolts. This
figure is consistent with prior measurements on copper substrates prepared by electropolishing,
though our value is somewhat lower than reports using as-received foil, which may reflect
differences in surface roughness rather than a genuine kinetic distinction.

## Discussion

The data support a nucleation-limited growth regime at low methane flux. A limitation of this study
is that substrate grain orientation was not independently characterized, so some of the observed
variance may be attributable to local crystallography rather than temperature alone. Future work
should pair electron backscatter diffraction with nucleation counts on the same foil to separate
these contributions. Within the tested range, higher temperature reliably favored larger domains,
a result of practical value for applications requiring low grain-boundary density.
